TECH2_2021-21.exp: The relationship runs the other way: every government service is supported by a set of processes, not every process supported by a set of services. The other three are standard process-orientation statements (processes rather than functions drive the organisation and are what satisfy stakeholders).

TECH2_2021-22.exp: Intra-government re-engineering reworks the internal workflows, file movement and approvals that citizens never see, which is by definition the back office. The front office is the citizen-facing delivery channel such as a portal or CSC counter.

TECH2_2021-23.exp: Merely computerizing existing processes is automation of the As-Is and is the classic anti-pattern GPR exists to prevent, since it hard-codes the inefficiency into software. Studying current functionality, drafting the To-Be and changing approval chains are all genuine GPR steps.

TECH2_2021-24.exp: Legacy manual processes carry redundant approvals, paper artefacts and non-standard steps that cannot simply be lifted into software, so they must be re-engineered to become automation ready. The other options describe staff or compliance grievances rather than the process rationale for GPR.

TECH2_2021-25.exp: Loopholes in the current system, redundant and lengthy approval chains, and communication gaps within government are all standard triggers for undertaking GPR. Each on its own is a recognised symptom, so all of them apply.

TECH2_2021-26.exp: Incremental, step-by-step improvement of existing processes using IT is Government Process Improvement; re-engineering by contrast means radical, fundamental redesign. Confusing improvement with re-engineering is the standard trap in this pair.

TECH2_2021-27.exp: Single-vendor (prime vendor) sourcing is the optimum choice when all externally sourced components can be bundled into one package under one point of accountability. Options A and C describe the multi-vendor model, which is what demands higher departmental capacity and carries coordination risk.

TECH2_2021-28.exp: In the standard model RFP structure, Volume I is Instructions to Bidders and covers the bid process, evaluation, negotiation and award of contract; Volume II carries functional and technical requirements and Volume III the draft MSA/SLA. Volume numbering does vary between departments, so this is model-dependent.

TECH2_2021-29.exp: A Request for Quotations is used where the requirement is fully standardized and specifications are settled, so selection reduces to the lowest quoted price. Rate contracts fix the price in advance rather than letting price decide, and single sourcing involves no price competition at all.

TECH2_2021-30.exp: GeM, the Government e-Marketplace, is the Government of India's online platform for procurement of common use goods and services by central and state government entities. The other two expansions are not real initiatives.

TECH2_2021-31.exp: Mass customization is the standard term for tailoring products or services to individual customers while retaining the economics of mass production. Specialization refers to narrowing what an organisation does, not to per-customer tailoring.

TECH2_2021-32.exp: Training and capacity building recurs through the project's operational life as staff turn over, modules change and refresher rounds are needed, so it is budgeted as a recurring cost. Digitization and migration, installation and configuration, and ERP customization are one-time capital or implementation-phase costs.

TECH2_2021-33.exp: Portal subscription charges, transaction fees on online services and advertising are the standard revenue streams an e-Governance initiative can generate. A CSC registration fee is an entry cost paid by the operator to join the network rather than a revenue stream the initiative creates, though the option set here is loosely drafted.

TECH2_2021-34.exp: In the conventional (departmental) model the government funds, builds, owns and operates the system itself, so it retains the whole of the risk and the whole of the return. Outsourcing, PPP and BOO(T) all exist precisely to transfer some share of risk and return to a private partner.

TECH2_2021-35.exp: A defining PPP principle is that government retains responsibility for and accountability over delivery of core services even when a private partner builds and operates the infrastructure. The classic PPP tenets also hold that government need not own the infrastructure and that PPP is about services rather than assets, which rules out A and D.

TECH2_2021-36.exp: Transferring construction and delivery risk to the private partner under a fixed-price, output-based contract reduces the government's exposure to cost overruns. The other options state the opposite of a benefit (maximised outgo, increased lifecycle costs) or are meaningless.

TECH2_2021-37.exp: BOOT stands for Build, Own, Operate, Transfer: the concessionaire builds and owns the asset, operates it for the concession period, then transfers ownership to government. The 'Buy' variants are not standard PPP acronyms.

TECH2_2021-38.exp: Mass market, niche market, segmented, diversified and multi-sided are the five standard types of Customer Segments in the Business Model Canvas. Value proposition, key resources and the canvas as a whole are separate blocks.

TECH2_2021-39.exp: Revenue stream types include asset sale, usage fee, subscription fee, lending/renting/leasing, licensing, brokerage fees and advertising. 'Value' is not a revenue stream; it belongs to the value proposition block and is the deliberate distractor.

TECH2_2021-40.exp: Key Resources are the assets, physical, intellectual, human or financial, required to create the value proposition, reach markets, sustain customer relationships and earn revenue. Key activities are what the firm does with those assets, not the assets themselves.
